titulo: Study Shows How Earth’s Orbit Affects Ice Ages

fuente.licencia: Dominio público (VOA, gobierno de EE. UU.)
fuente.nota: Texto recortado por párrafos; sin cambios en las frases.

parrafos: A group of scientists studied changes in the shape of the Earth’s orbit around the sun, the tilt of the Earth’s axis and the movement of the axis itself, called a wobble. These three motions are believed to happen in cycles. The Serbian scientist Milutin Milankovitch developed a theory about 100 years ago that these cycles affected Earth’s long-term climate.
The team noted that small changes in Earth’s orbit around the Sun caused predictable cycles of warming and cooling over a period of about 100,000 years.
These findings permitted the team to determine how the three factors of tilt, wobble, and the shape of Earth's orbit might have affected the Earth’s climate over the last 900,000 years.

The lead writer of the study is Stephen Barker, a professor at Cardiff University in Britain. He told the French News Agency (AFP) that for many years it has been difficult for scientists to show exactly how small changes in Earth’s orbit have led to huge changes between warm and cold periods.

Earth is believed to go through cycles of ice ages and warm periods. The last ice age is thought to have ended around 11,700 years ago. Scientists, such as Milankovitch, have long seen a connection between Earth's orbit and climate.

However, researchers have struggled to precisely date when each of the climate changes happened. It has also been difficult for them to know exactly which orbit positions affect the start and stop of cold or warm periods.
Barker said his team of researchers studied slow changes in temperature over long periods of time instead of only looking at shorter periods of change between cold and warm climates.

Lorraine Lisiecki is a professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and a co-writer of the study. She said the study shows that changes in climate over tens of thousands of years are not random.
The team aims to expand its findings to investigate the long-term effects of human activity on climate. They also want to find out how it might affect Earth’s natural climate cycles.
titulo_es: Un estudio muestra cómo la órbita de la Tierra influye en las glaciaciones
resumen_es: Un equipo científico confirma que los cambios de la órbita y del eje de la Tierra determinan de forma predecible los ciclos de glaciaciones y periodos cálidos, como propuso Milankovitch hace un siglo.

ideas_clave.idea: Scientists examined three cyclical movements of the Earth, which Milankovitch linked to long-term climate a century ago.
They found that small orbital changes produce predictable warming and cooling cycles of about 100,000 years, allowing them to reconstruct climate over 900,000 years.
Until now it had been hard to prove how minor orbital variations trigger huge shifts between warm and cold periods.
Although the link between orbit and climate was long suspected, dating each change and identifying the decisive orbital positions had proved difficult.
By studying slow temperature changes over long periods, the team showed that climate shifts over tens of millennia are not random.
The researchers now intend to study how human activity may alter these natural cycles.

resumen_modelo: The text presents a study on how the Earth's movements around the sun influence ice ages. A team of scientists analysed three cyclical factors: the shape of the planet's orbit, the tilt of its axis and the wobble of that axis, building on the theory proposed a century ago by the Serbian scientist Milutin Milankovitch. Their results indicate that slight variations in the orbit generate predictable cycles of warming and cooling lasting roughly 100,000 years, which enabled them to reconstruct the climate of the last 900,000 years. This is significant because, although a connection between orbit and climate had long been suspected, scientists had struggled to date each change precisely and to identify which orbital positions trigger the beginning or end of cold and warm periods. Unlike earlier work, the team focused on gradual temperature changes over long periods, concluding that long-term climate variations are not random. Finally, the researchers plan to extend their findings to examine the long-term impact of human activity on the climate and its natural cycles.
